The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused persons have violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules.

The accused no. 1 is stated to be the vendor of M/s. D. L. Narula Fruit Products, of which accused no. 2 is the proprietor, from whose premises the food article, that is, 'vegetable sauce' was lifted for sampling.

2. As per the complaint, on 06.03.2009, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) R. K.
Bhaskar and Field Assistant (FA) Om Prakash under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. Aashish Mohan reached along with their staff at the premises of M/s. D. L. Narula Food Products, at Khasra No. 76, Village Ranhola, Nangloi, Delhi, where the accused no. 1 was found conducting business of the food articles and having stored for sale for human consumption "vegetable sauce" in sealed glass bottles of 400 gms each bearing identical label declaration.

sentences.text: The sample of three such sealed glass bottles was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.

Each sample was separately packed, fastened,
marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the Notice as per Form-VI, panchnama, etc.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.
Vide report dated 30.03.2009, the PA found the sample to be not conforming to the standards because acidity as acetic acid was less than the prescribed minimum limit.
Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by the FI.
It was found that the accused no. 2 was the proprietor of the business concern M/s. D. L. Narula Fruit Products and the product was being manufactured by the said concern itself.
After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.
The complaint was then filed in the court against both the accused persons on 06.08.2009 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act, as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned vide order dated 06.08.2009.

The accused persons appeared and filed an application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising right to get the second counterpart of the sample to be analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
The application was allowed and a counterpart was sent for analysis to CFL.

The CFL examined the sample and its Director gave Certificate dated 11.09.2009, opining the sample to be not conforming to the PFA Rules as acidity as acetic acid content was less than the minimum prescribed limit.

4. Based on the report of the CFL, notice of accusation under section 251 CrPC was framed against both the accused persons on 16.12.2009 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a), being violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
5. At the trial, prosecution examined three witnesses in support of its case.

PW-1 FI R. K. Bhaskar,
PW-2 Sh. Aashish Mohan (SDM/LHA) and PW-3 FA Om Prakash were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings.

All these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 06.03.2009 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of three sealed glass bottles 400 gms each of Vegetable Sauce bearing identical label declaration, dividing it in three parts by putting ine sealed bottle as one counterpart,
separately packing, fastening, sealing, marking the sample bottles, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex.
PW-1/A, cash memo Ex. PW-1/A-1, Notice in Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B (on which the vendor made endorsement that the samples were of same lot, having same batch number, having same date of manufacturing and ready for sale), Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C and Raid report Ex. PW-1/C1.
The vendor accused no. 1 also furnished her statement Ex. PW-1/D and the FI also separately seized the label of the bottle Ex. PW-1/D1.

They also proved the PA Receipt Ex. PW-1/E and LHA receipt Ex.
PW-1/F vide which the samples were deposited with the PA and SDM/LHA respectively.

sentences.text: Ex. PW-1/G was received and investigation was started by FI PW-1 who sent letter Ex. PW-1/H to the STO Ward No. 62 received its reply.
After completion of investigation, sanction Ex. PW-1/I was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex. PW-1/J was filed in the court.
A copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-1/K was sent to the accused persons through post vide receipt Ex. PW-1/L.

These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel wherein they denied that the accused no. 1 did not sign the documents ir had signed under duress, or that the three samples were not of the same batch number, lot number or colour, or that representative samples were not taken, or that the accused persons had been falsely implicated.
6. Statements of the accused persons under section 313 CrPC were recorded on 23.02.2015 wherein they denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
Accused no. 1 admitted the proceedings dated 06.03.2009 but stated that no effort was made to join public witnesses.
She claimed that she did not accept price of the sample commodity as the sauce was not for public sale.
Accused no. 2 on the other hand expressed ignorance about the proceedings stating that he was not present at the spot.
They disputed the correctness of PA and CFL reports on the ground that they are at variance.
They however did not lead any evidence in defence.

7. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against both the accused persons beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that they have not been able to rebut the findings of the CFL report dated 11.09.2009 which as per section 13(3) and (5) of PFA Act is final and conclusive.
It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony.

8. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various contradictions and missing links in the testimony of witnesses.
Ld. Counsel has contended that proper methodology was not adopted by the analysts for detecting adulteration.
It is argued that there is variation in the PA report and CFL report which shows that representative samples were not taken.

Ld. Counsel has also pointed out that the PA had analysed the sample under Item no. A.16.12 of Appendix-B of PFA Rules as "Fruit Products" but the CFL analysed the sample under Item no. A.16.28(ii) as "Vegetable Sauce" which shows that the samples were not same.

He has also pointed out that the PA found the colour of sample to be red but the CFL found the same to be greenish, and has contended that this would create a doubt as to the samples being that of the same article.
9. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused persons and have carefully perused the material available on record.
10. It is to be understood that the notice framed against the accused persons is for violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of the PFA Act.

Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature, substance or quality which it purported or represented to be. Section 2(ia)(m)
of PFA Act deals with situation where the quality or purity of an article falls below the prescribed standard or its constituents are present in quantities not within the prescribed limits of variability.

sentences.text: To begin with, it is seen that an issue has been raised by the Ld. Defence Counsel with respect to identity of the product, particularly in view of the divergent observations of the PA and CFL.

It is a matter of record that as per the PA report, the sample was "NFP vegetable sauce sample in originally sealed glass bottle", its physical appearance showed "red coloured sample of sauce" and it was considered as a "Fruit Product"
falling under Item No. A.16.12 of Appendix-B of PFA Rules. The opinion given by PA is "the sample does not conform to the standard because acidity as acetic acid is less than the prescribed minimum limit of 1.2%"
(it was found to be 0.80%).

However, perusal of the CFL report would show that the sample was "NFP vegetable sauce" received in "sealed company glass bottle", its physical appearance showed "greenish coloured, Vegetable Sauce" and it was considered as a "Vegetable Sauce"
falling under Item No. A.16.28(ii) of Appendix-B of PFA Rules.

The opinion given by CFL is "the above sample contains Acidity less than 1.2% & hence does not conforms to the standards of Fruits & Vegetable Sauces other than Tomato and Soya Sauce i.e.
Chilly Sauce as per PFA Rules" (it was found to be 0.74%).
12.
Ignoring the differences for the time being, it is important to note that both the PA and CFL found the sample to be that of "Vegetable Sauce".

Both the samples were bearing the label "NFP Vegetable Sauce"
which is in conformity with the label seized separately by the FI as Ex. PW-1/D1.
All the PWs have deposed that the three sealed bottles were lifted for sampling and one sealed bottle was considered as one counterpart.
The PA and CFL reports would confirm that the analysts had received such originally sealed glass bottles.
Thus, there was no tampering in the same.

13. The chances of tampering in the sample or its being changed by the food officials, without the knowledge, connivance or consent of the accused, have been virtually made impossible by the amendment of 1976 in the PFA Act.
The FI is required to obtain the signatures of the accused vendor on the samples when lifted as per section 11(b).

Subsequently, after PA report is received and prosecution is instituted, its copy is sent to the accused with information that the accused can apply to the court within ten days to get the second counterpart analysed through CFL.

If such application is made, the court requires the LHA to produce the counterparts of the sample to be produced before it and as per section 13(2B), the court ascertains that the mark and seal are intact and signatures are not tampered with.
After such satisfaction, the sample is sent for analysis to the CFL.
14. In the case at hand, after the prosecution was instituted on 06.08.2009, intimation was sent to the accused persons.
They moved an application under section 13(2) for getting the counterpart of sample analysed through CFL.
On this application, vide order dared 21.08.2009, the court called for the samples through LHA.
On 26.08.2009, samples were produced by the LHA and court observed that they were properly packed, marked and sealed.

The accused gave statement on 26.08.2009 that Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Smt. Divya Narula on 16 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/92022287/
4 the counterparts were properly packed, fastened, marked and sealed, that signatures of vendor appeared thereupon, and that the seals were intact.

sentences.text: The court also compared the signatures of the vendor as appearing on counterpart with the statutory documents and also found that there was no tampering in the seal.
It was only thereafter that the court sent the counterpart to the CFL for analysis.
15. What follows is, that whatever counterparts had been sealed by the FI at the spot, they were produced before the court and the accused was also satisfied that the seals were intact.
There was no scope of changing the samples when the same were in the custody of the food officials, as they bore signatures of the accused as well.
The sample could not have been changed without disturbing the seals and signatures of the vendor.
And in this case, the accused vendor had checked and satisfied herself about the seals and signatures being intact and without any tampering when the counterparts were produced in the court.
So, the possibility of change in samples stands ruled out.

16. Now, instead of going into the question as to what the sample commodity actually was, the court is more concerned with as to what the sample commodity was "represented to be" (as per the wordings of section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act).
It is important to note that the accused persons have nowhere questioned the correctness of the label seized by the FI Ex. PW- 1/D1.
This label states "NFP Vegetable Sauce" on it as the description of the product.
This label bears the complete name and address of the business concern M/s. D. L. Narula Fruit Products as manufacturer.
It is nowhere the stand of the defence that this label is a forged or duplicate one.
Even the contents of label as reproduced by the FI on Notice in Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B shows that the sample was stated to be that of vegetable sauce.

As per the detailed endorsement made by the accused no.1 on Ex. PW-1/B in her own handwriting, the sealed glass bottles of 'vegetable sauce' of NFP Brand were of same batch number and manufacturing date.

This fact was reiterated by the vendor in her statement Ex.
PW-1/D.
Again, as per the invoice/cash memo Ex. PW- 1/A1 issued by the vendor herself with respect to receipt of price of the sample, the product description was mentioned as "3 x 400 gm vegetable sauce".
Even at the trial, the accused persons never disputed the fact that the product was or was represented to be "vegetable sauce".

It follows that irrespective of what the product actually was in the sample bottles, it was 'represented to be' a vegetable sauce and was thus required to be tested as per the standards of vegetable sauce only.
17. The court cannot still ignore the fact that as per the PA report, the sample appeared to be red in colour, but as per the CFL report, it was greenish in colour.
All the PWs during evidence stated that the product appeared to be red in colour when lifted.

There can be no explainable reason how the colour of the sample changed from red to greenish (not green), except that due to passage of time,
its ingredients underwent some change that resulted in change in colour as well.
The natural colours are prone to various changes (as against synthetic colours).
The sample was analysed by the CFL from 05.09.2009 to 11.09.2009, that is, after six months when it was lifted.

During this intervening period, there might have been some changes in the composition of the product that resulted in change of its colour, particularly when the possibility of change in sample has been ruled out.

18. And if not, then it would follow that the product was not of the same nature, substance or quality despite being sold under the same name, same batch number, same lot and same manufacturing Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Smt. sentences.text: As per the prosecution case, the product was bearing identical label declaration.
The label declarations reproduced by the FI on Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B tally with the declaration on original label Ex. PW- 1/D1.

The accused vendor also furnished her statement at the spot, in her own handwriting, on both Ex. PW-1/B and Ex. PW-1/D to the effect that the sealed bottles were of same batch number and same manufacturing date, that were being manufactured by them and were ready for sale.
The batch number '04' appearing on Ex. PW-1/B also tallies with batch number mentioned on Ex. PW-1/D1 (though handwritten).

The accused never led any evidence to establish that the samples were of different products or were of different batches/lot or bearing different batch numbers or were without batch number (which is also an offence of misbranding) or were of different manufacturing dates, except putting bald suggestion to this effect to PW-2 which he vehemently denied.
No such stand was taken by the accused persons in their statements under section 313 CrPC nor any such fact was proved through any defence witness.

19. Similarly, there is no evidence to establish the stand of the accused that she did not sign the documents prepared at the spot or that the FI himself signed the documents or that the statement Ex. PW-1/D1 was made under duress, as suggested to PW-1.
Both the stands are apparently contradictory.
If the accused claims that she did not sign any document or that the FI had signed them, there was no occasion for her to claim that she had signed under duress.
Be that as it may, no such stand has been taken by the accused in her statement under section 313 CrPC.
No suggestion to this effect was put to PW-2 or PW-3.

No evidence in defence was led to establish that the signatures and handwriting on documents prepared at the spot (which are claimed to be in handwriting of accused no. 1) belonged to the FI or any other person, though nay handwriting or forensic expert.
This is more so when the accused even accepted on 26.08.2009 that her signatures on the samples were intact.
No compliant alleging such forgery has been lodged by her against the FI in any forum whatsoever.
Rather her signatures appearing on the documents prepared at the spot tally with her signatures on her statement under section 313 CrPC (which cannot be denied by her) when compared with naked eyes.
Thus, her stands that she did not sign the documents or made statement under duress, appear to be without merit and afterthought which are liable to be rejected.
20. At this stage, it is to be understood that ordinarily, the food officials are required to homogenize the sample so as to make them truly representative.
Such homogenization is to ensure that all the ingredients of the sample article are distributed evenly so that there is nil or minimal variation in the two samples.

For instance, if a sample of flour is lifted, it is required that it is mixed properly and homogenized so that its ingredients like moisture, ash content, extraneous matter, etc. are uniformly distributed.
And if not so homogenized, there is possibility that one counterpart gets some ingredient in excess and the other gets that ingredient in deficiency.
That would obviously not give proper results.
21. On this basis, Ld. Counsel submits that the sample proceedings were not proper.
It is claimed that the FI did not homogenize the contents of the food article.

Ld. Counsel has contended that the proper method would have been to open the three bottles, transfer its contents into a single container, properly homogenize it, then divide it into three parts and the seal and pack them separately.

sentences.text: Well, there is no merit in such contention.
The above rule of homogenization would be subject to the "Note" to Rule 22 of the PFA Rules.

It states "Food sold in packed condition (sealed container or package) shall be sent for analysis in its original condition, without opening the package as far as practicable, to constitute approximate quantity alongwith original label."

Thus, if the food article is being sold in packed condition, as in the present case where sealed bottles were there, the FI could not have opened the bottles and mixed its contents as being claimed, as that would have resulted in violation of Rule 22.

If the sealed bottles were bearing identical label declaration, thus represented to be of the same lot and batch, the FI was required to lift them in the same condition only without opening the original package.

It was rather for the accused to ensure that such products containing same product, bearing same label, bearing same batch/lot number and same manufacturing date,
are of the same nature, substance and quality in all the sealed containers.

It would be rather a violation of Rules if an accused is selling different product or same product but of different qualities,
under the same batch number and same label declarations, as that would amount to misleading declarations.

23. Thus, as far as the present case is concerned, since the product was "represented to be" vegetable sauce for same batch/lot, it was required to be lifted accordingly and analysed accordingly,
irrespective of the fact what actually were its ingredients.

The court is now required to ascertain if the product was of the nature, quality and substance which it purported or represented to be, that is,
vegetable sauce.

24. It is to be noted that "Vegetable Sauce" is a standardized food article, which falls in Item no.
A.16.28 of the Appendix B of PFA Rules, as "Culinary Paste/Fruits and Vegetable Sauces other than Tomato Sauce and Soya Sauce" under the main head "Fruit Products" (A.16).

Detailed standards have been prescribed with respect to such "Fruits/Vegetable Sauces" in clause (2) of Item No.
A.16.28(2).
Such vegetable sauce requires Total Soluble Solids (Salt free basis) to be not less than 15.0% and Acidity (as acetic acid) to be not less than 1.2%.

25. The record however shows that the PA in her report has mentioned the food article to be falling in Item no. A.16.12 as "Fruit products", though the CFL has correctly mentioned the same to be falling in Item no. A.16.28(ii) as "Vegetable Sauce".

Apparently, the PA has wrongly mentioned the Item number under which the product "Vegetable Sauce" is falling, as Item no. A.16.12 deals with "Thermally Processed Fruit Pulp/ Puree and sweetened Fruit Pulp/Puree other than Mango".
It is Item no. A.16.28 only that pertains to the food article "Vegetable Sauce".

Since the PA has not been examined on record (as her report stands superseded by the CFL certificate), no reason could be ascertained as to why and how she had wrongly mentioned the Item number in her report.
26. However, no benefit can be given to the accused solely on this count.

This is primarily because other than mentioning of wrong Item number, there is no fault or irregularity in the tests conducted and also the standards on which the results have been evaluated by the analysis.

Both the reports clearly show that the food article had been analysed for presence of acidity to be not less than 15%
and total soluble solids to be not less than 1.2%.

These standards have been mentioned only in Item no. A.16.28 and have not been prescribed in Item no. A.16.12 which prescribes total soluble solids as not less than 6.0% and acidity as citric acid (not as acetic acid) as not less than 0.3%.

It is therefore Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Smt. Divya Narula on 16 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/92022287/
7 not a case where the product was analysed on standards of some other product.

sentences.text: The last column of analysis reports in both the reports clearly mentions the prescribed standards of vegetable sauce as provided under Item no. A.16.28(2) only.
The food article was never evaluated on the basis of detailed standards prescribed under Item no. A.16.12, as mentioned in the PA report.
Rather both the analysis have given specific "opinion" at the end of their respective reports finding that the sample did not conform to the standards as acidity was found less than 1.2%.

It is therefore clear that PA had wrongly mentioned the Item number under which the food product fell, though the standards applied to the sampled commodity were correct and the opinion had been given on the basis of correct prescribed standards as per Item no. A.16.28.
27.
In any case, the court is not bound by the Item number mentioned by the PA in its report, as the court is primarily concerned with the results given by the analysts on the basis of chemical analysis.

Since the parameters applied to the food product were correct and as per the prescribed standards,
no benefit can be given to the accused on this count.
In any case, the report of PA stands superseded in view of section 13(3) and (5) of the PFA Act by the CFL certificate which is final and conclusive.
28. It is pertinent to note that the PA found the presence acidity less than the minimum prescribed limits in the sample analysed.
And this fact has been confirmed even by the CFL which also found the same deficiency in the second sample.
Thus, this is one of the few cases where the reports of CFL and PA are in conformity to each other.
29. But Ld. Defence Counsel still argues that the reports are at variance.
It is pointed out that as per PA report, total soluble solids were 25.06% and total acidity was 0.80%.
But as per CFL report, total soluble solids were 23.66% and total acidity was 0.74%.
On this basis, the defence is seeking to claim that the samples were not representative due to said 'variations of more than 0.3%' in total soluble solids content in PA and CFL reports.

State [2005(2) FAC 219].
In view of the defence taken, it is necessary to understand the concept of reports of PA and CFL and variations therein.
32. As per section 13(3) of the PFA Act, the certificate issued by the Director of CFL shall supersede the report of the PA.

As per proviso to section 13(5) of the Act, such certificate shall be final and Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Smt. Divya Narula on 16 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/92022287/

sentences.text: Thus, as far as the findings of the CFL are concerned, the same are final and conclusive and no evidence can be given to disprove the same.

33. In Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738], it has been authoritatively laid down that the legal impact of a certificate of the Director of CFL is three fold: (a)
it annuls or replaces the report of the PA, (b) it gains finality regarding the quality and standard of the food article involved in the case and (c) it becomes irrefutable so far as the facts stated therein are concerned.

sentences.text: In Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100], it was observed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi that "It has repeatedly been held by the supreme court that the certificate of the Director supersedes the report of the public analyst and is to be treated as conclusive evidence of its contents.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Director is a greater expert and therefore the statute says that his certificate shall be accepted by the court as conclusive evidence.
For all purposes the report of the public analyst is replaced by the certificate of the Director....
Superseded is a strong word.
It means obliterate, set aside, annul, replace, make void, inefficacious or useless, repeal.
The Director's certificate supersedes the report given by the public analyst.
Once superseded it does not survive for any purpose.

It is thus clear that the Kanshi Nath and Bishan Sarup judgements are on the same lines.
There can be no dispute that if there are such variations on the basis of which the accused is able to show that the samples were not representative, the accused would be given benefit.
However, the important point to be noted is, that there is no rule prescribed under the statute to conclude what variation would be "substantial enough" to be considered in favour of the accused.

The Act or Rules do not prescribe that there any variation of more than a specific value / percentage would be a substantial variation so as to disregard the report of the CFL which has otherwise been given finality and conclusiveness.

In the absence of any such standard prescribed, the matter would be governed only by the evidence adduced by the parties, which includes cross-examination of complainant's witnesses and/or examination of defence witnesses (subject to cross-examination of course).

If the accused on the basis of evidence can show that any particular variation, to a particular extent, in any particular matter and for a particular ingredient, would be "substantial enough", then certainly he would be given benefit.

sentences.text: Section 7 of the PFA Act specifies it clearly that "No person shall himself or by any person on his behalf manufacture for sale or store, sell or distribute... (i) any adulterated food...".
Thus, both the vendor and the proprietor would be covered under purview of the PFA Act and a vendor cannot take the ground that only the proprietor would be liable.
67. No other stand has been taken by the accused persons at the trial or during the arguments advanced.

68. The case in hand would be covered under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act as there is evidence to show that the food article was not of the nature, substance or quality which it is "purported" to be as per PFA Rules and "represented to be" by the accused.
The case would also fall under section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act as the constituents of acidity as acetic acid was present in quantities not upto the prescribed minimum limits as per the PFA Rules.

Certainly, it cannot be said that the said deficiency was affecting injuriously the nature, substance or quality of the product or was injurious to health, and that is the reason why the accused persons are not facing trial for violation of section 2(ia)(b) or (h).

Violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) is punishable under section 16(i)(a) of PFA Act.
69.

In view of this discussion, it can be said that the complainant / prosecution has been able to establish its case and prove the guilt of both the accused persons beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt.

It has been proved that the accused persons had sold or caused to be sold an adulterated food in violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act, and have committed the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) of the PFA Act.
70.

Having said so, both the accused persons are held guilty and are convicted for the offence punishable under section 16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
